920:
An appliance is a device or machine that is purpose-built to perform a specific, practical task — usually to make everyday life easier, more comfortable, or more efficient. The word almost always implies that the device does something useful, repeatedly and reliably, by using some form of power (most commonly electricity) or mechanical action.

Think of it this way: an appliance is not just any random object. It is something that was designed with a job in mind.
The Most Common Use: Home Appliances

When most people hear the word "appliance," they think of the machines found in a home that help with everyday chores and living. These are called household appliances or home appliances, and they fall into two broad groups:

Large appliances (sometimes called "white goods" in the industry) are the big, heavy machines that usually stay in one fixed place. Examples include:

  • A refrigerator — keeps food cold and fresh
  • A washing machine — cleans clothes
  • A dishwasher — cleans dishes
  • An oven or stove — cooks food
  • A dryer — dries wet clothes after washing

Small appliances are the compact, countertop machines that can be moved around more easily. Examples include:

  • A toaster — toasts bread
  • A blender — mixes or liquifies food and drinks
  • A microwave — heats food quickly using microwave radiation
  • A coffee maker — brews coffee
  • An electric kettle — boils water

What all of these have in common is that they save you time and physical effort. Without them, you would have to do the same job by hand — washing clothes by hand, boiling water over a fire, and so on. An appliance takes over that effort for you.
Beyond the Home: Other Types of Appliances

The word is not limited to the kitchen or laundry room. It is used in other fields too, whenever a device is specifically built to do a defined job for a person.

Medical appliances are devices used to support, assist, or improve a person's body and health. Examples include:

  • A hearing aid — helps a person with hearing loss to hear
  • A prosthetic limb — replaces a missing arm or leg
  • An orthopedic brace — supports a weak or injured joint, like a knee brace

Dental appliances are devices used in the care and treatment of teeth and the mouth. Examples include:

  • Braces — gradually straighten teeth over time
  • A retainer — keeps teeth in place after braces are removed
  • Dentures — a full set of artificial teeth for someone who has lost their natural ones
  • A night guard (mouthguard) — worn during sleep to prevent teeth grinding

In all these cases, the same logic applies: it is a device, engineered for a specific purpose, used on or by a person to perform that purpose.
The One Idea That Ties It All Together

No matter the context, an appliance always has these qualities:

  1. It is designed for a specific function. It was built to do one job (or a small set of related jobs), not anything and everything.
  2. It operates with some form of power or mechanism. It is not a passive object like a plate or a chair. It does something — it heats, cools, cleans, mixes, supports, or corrects.
  3. It is used regularly and repeatedly. An appliance is not a one-time-use thing. It is meant to be part of your daily or ongoing life.
  4. It replaces or assists human effort. This is its fundamental value — it does work that a person would otherwise have to do themselves, or it does something a person physically cannot do alone (like a prosthetic limb or a hearing aid).

Since you are a learner, it helps to understand where this word sits among words that sound similar.

Tool — A tool is usually simpler, often hand-powered, and requires the user to provide all the physical effort. A hammer, a screwdriver, or a knife are tools. They have no internal power source. An appliance, by contrast, typically has a power source and does much of the work itself.

Machine — This is a broader word. All appliances are machines, but not all machines are appliances. A car is a machine, but it is not usually called an appliance. A large factory press is a machine, not an appliance. Appliances are a specific category of machines — the kind used by individuals or households for personal, domestic, or medical purposes.

Device — This is even broader than "machine" and covers almost anything made to serve a purpose, including electronic gadgets, clocks, sensors, and so on. An appliance is a type of device, but a much more specific one.

Gadget — This word often implies something small, clever, and sometimes a little frivolous or novelty-focused. An appliance, by contrast, has a serious and practical function. A toaster is an appliance. A tiny keychain bottle-opener might be called a gadget.

Instrument — This word typically implies precision and is most used in science, medicine, and music (a surgical instrument, a musical instrument, a measuring instrument). There is some overlap with "medical appliance," but an instrument usually implies something more precise and skill-dependent in its use.

In older or more formal English writing, "appliance" can occasionally mean the act of applying something — that is, the use or deployment of a principle, skill, or method. For example, the phrase "the appliance of science" means "the application of science" or "putting science to practical use." This sense is uncommon in everyday modern English, but you may encounter it in older texts or formal writing. In nearly all modern usage, you can safely assume "appliance" refers to a device or machine.

An appliance is a powered device or machine that is purpose-built to perform a specific, practical task — most commonly a household machine like a refrigerator or washing machine, but also a medical device like a hearing aid or a dental device like braces. The word always carries the idea of something designed with a clear job to do, something that works for you by reducing or replacing human effort.
921:
When something is applicable, it means it is relevant, suitable, or fitting for a specific situation, person, or case — in other words, it actually applies to that situation. Think of it as asking: "Does this belong here? Does this fit this situation?" If yes, then it is applicable.

Imagine you have a set of rules for a swimming pool. The rule "no running on the pool deck" is applicable to everyone who visits the pool. But the rule "no diving" might only be applicable to the shallow end. The rules fit and are relevant to those specific situations.

The word is almost always used to describe whether a rule, law, idea, method, concept, or piece of information can meaningfully connect to or be used in a given context.

There are two key things happening when something is "applicable":

1. It is relevant — it actually relates to the situation at hand. It is not off-topic or disconnected.

2. It can be put into practice or enforced — it is not just related in a vague way; it genuinely works for, or applies to, the specific case.

Both things must be true. Something that is applicable is not just loosely connected — it fits, it counts, and it matters in that specific situation.

Here are examples across different areas of life, so you can see how the word behaves:

Law and rules:
"This law is applicable to all businesses with more than 50 employees."
→ The law fits and must be followed by those businesses. It is relevant and enforceable for them.

Advice and guidance:
"This skincare advice is only applicable to people with dry skin."
→ If you have oily skin, this advice does not fit your situation. It does not apply to you.

Work and forms:
"Please answer only the questions that are applicable to your situation."
→ Some questions on the form may not relate to you at all. Skip those; only answer the ones that fit your case.

Science and methods:
"This research method is widely applicable across many fields of study."
→ The method is flexible and relevant in many different contexts — not just one.

Discounts and offers:
"This coupon is applicable only on weekdays."
→ The discount fits and can be used only during weekdays. On weekends, it does not apply.

You will very commonly see "not applicable" or its abbreviation "N/A" in forms, documents, and surveys. This simply means: "This question or item does not relate to this person or situation."

For example, if a form asks for your "spouse's name" and you are unmarried, you write "N/A" — because that question is not applicable to you. It simply does not fit your situation.

This is one of the most practical uses of the word, and understanding it will help you immediately in everyday life.

Applicable is not the same as "useful" or "good." Something can be applicable — meaning it genuinely fits and relates to a situation — without being the best solution. A rule can be applicable to you even if you dislike it. The word is neutral; it simply tells you whether something fits and belongs, not whether it is beneficial.

Applicable often implies a condition or a scope. When you use this word, there is almost always an implied "to something" or "in some situation." A rule is applicable to a group. A method is applicable in a context. A law is applicable to a case. This is why you will often see "applicable to" used together as a phrase.

Applicable can be used in the positive or negative. You will see both "this is applicable" (it fits) and "this is not applicable" (it does not fit) used very frequently. Both are equally natural.

Widely applicable vs. narrowly applicable. Something that is widely applicable works across many situations. Something that is narrowly applicable only fits in a very specific, limited situation. This spectrum is useful to keep in mind.

These words share overlapping territory with "applicable," which will help sharpen your understanding:

Relevant — also means connected to the situation, but "relevant" is broader and more casual. "Applicable" carries a stronger sense of can be put into use or enforced, not just is related to.

Pertinent — means directly related and to the point. Very similar to relevant, but slightly more formal.

Appropriate — means fitting or suitable, but more about tone, manners, or conduct. You would say a rule is "applicable," not that it is "appropriate," unless you are judging whether it is the right rule morally or socially.

Valid — means something is legitimate and holds up. A rule can be valid (it exists and is legitimate) but still not applicable to your situation.

None of these fully replace "applicable" because "applicable" specifically highlights the idea that something fits and can be applied to a given case — it carries that sense of a direct connection between a rule/concept/method and a real situation.

Inapplicable — the direct opposite. It means something does not fit or is not relevant to the situation.

Irrelevant — means it has no connection to the situation at all.

Moot — in certain contexts, means something has no practical application (though "moot" has more specific legal meanings too).

"Applicable" is a moderately formal word. You will encounter it often in legal documents, official forms, workplace policies, academic writing, and instructions. In casual conversation, people are more likely to say "this applies to you" or "this is relevant to you" rather than "this is applicable to you." However, "applicable" is not so formal that it sounds strange in regular conversation — it is perfectly natural in both spoken and written English.

"Applicable" means that something — a rule, law, idea, method, or piece of information — is relevant and suitable enough to fit, count, or be used in a specific situation or for a specific person.

If something is applicable, it belongs there. If it is not applicable, it has no business being there — it does not fit, does not relate, and should be set aside.
922: An applicant is a person who formally requests something — usually an opportunity, a position, a benefit, or a permission — from an authority or organization that has the power to grant or deny it. The key word here is formally. An applicant doesn't just casually ask; they go through an official process, typically by filling out a form, submitting documents, or completing some kind of structured request. That official process is called an application, and the act of doing it is to apply. So: you apply → you submit an application → you become an applicant.

Whenever someone becomes an applicant, there are always two sides. On one side is the applicant — the person who wants something. On the other side is an organization, institution, or authority — the one who decides. The applicant is essentially saying, "I would like this thing, and here is the information you need to decide whether I qualify." The organization then reviews the request and either accepts or rejects it. Being an applicant does not mean you will get what you asked for — it simply means you have formally entered the process of trying to get it.
Where you will see this word

"Applicant" appears in many common real-life situations. A person applying for a job is a job applicant. A student applying to a university is a college applicant. Someone requesting a loan from a bank is a loan applicant. A person applying for a visa to enter a country is a visa applicant. Someone seeking a grant (funding money) is a grant applicant. Someone requesting a patent (legal protection for an invention) is a patent applicant. In all these cases, the pattern is exactly the same: a person formally requests something, and an authority decides.
The timeline of being an applicant

It helps to understand when someone is called an applicant. A person becomes an applicant the moment they submit — or are in the process of submitting — their formal request. They remain an applicant while their request is being reviewed. Once a decision is made, the label usually changes. If accepted for a job, the applicant becomes an employee. If accepted into a university, the applicant becomes a student. If rejected, they are simply an unsuccessful applicant. The word "applicant" lives in that in-between stage — after the request has been made, but before the outcome is known.

Two words are often confused with "applicant": candidate and petitioner.

A candidate is very similar to an applicant, and in everyday conversation — especially in job-seeking situations — the two words are often used interchangeably. However, there is a subtle difference. "Candidate" tends to suggest someone who is actively being considered, possibly already shortlisted or evaluated. "Applicant" is broader and simply refers to anyone who has applied, regardless of how far along in the process they are. Think of it this way: all candidates may have once been applicants, but not all applicants become candidates.

A petitioner is someone who makes a formal request too, but this word is mostly used in legal and official government contexts — for example, someone asking a court for a ruling, or someone formally requesting a government authority to act on something.
Plural form and usage in sentences

The plural of applicant is simply applicants. Here are clear example sentences to show how the word is naturally used:

"The company received over 300 applicants for a single position."
"Every applicant must bring a valid ID to the interview."
"She was the most qualified applicant in the entire pool."
"The scholarship committee will review all applicants by the end of the month."
"As an applicant, you will be notified of the decision within two weeks."

If you ever need to recall this word quickly: an applicant is a person who has formally requested something — a job, a spot, a visa, a loan, or any other opportunity — and is waiting to find out if their request has been accepted.
923: "Application" is a word that wears many hats. It has five distinct meanings in English, but they all share a single underlying idea: directing something toward a target — whether that's a request, a substance, a skill, an effort, or a tool. Once you grasp that idea, all the meanings click into place naturally.

This is the most common use. When you officially ask an organization or authority for something — a job, a university seat, a visa, a passport, a loan — the process of asking, and the form you fill out, is called an application.

  • "She submitted her job application on Monday."
  • "His visa application was rejected."
  • "I filled out the college application carefully."

The key idea: you are formally putting your name forward and asking for something. You are applying to someone — and that act of applying is the application.
Meaning 2: The Act of Putting Something Onto a Surface or Body

"Application" can mean the physical act of placing, spreading, or pressing something onto something else. You'll see this in medicine, skincare, painting, and technical fields.

  • "The doctor suggested the application of an ice pack to reduce swelling."
  • "The application of a second coat of paint gave the wall an even finish."
  • "Repeat the application of the ointment twice daily."

Here, "application" simply means the act of applying — of putting one thing on another. It's a noun form of the verb "apply" in its most literal sense.
Meaning 3: The Practical Use of Something

When a theory, rule, law, skill, or idea is actually used in the real world — put into action — that use is called an application. The plural "applications" refers to the various real-world uses something has.

  • "This scientific principle has applications in aerospace engineering."
  • "The application of this rule to online fraud is still being debated."
  • "The research looks promising, but it has no practical application yet."

Think of it as the bridge between knowing something and using it. A law exists on paper; its application is what happens when a judge uses it in a courtroom. A formula exists in a textbook; its application is when an engineer uses it to build a bridge.

In everyday modern language, an application means a piece of software — a program built to perform a specific task on a computer, phone, or tablet. This is where the word "app" comes from; it's simply a shortening of "application."

  • "Microsoft Word is a word-processing application."
  • "She downloaded a budgeting application on her phone."
  • "The company developed a new application for managing deliveries."

Whether it's a game, a photo editor, a banking program, or a navigation tool — any software designed to do a particular job is called an application. The logic is the same: the software is a tool applied to a specific task.

This meaning is less common today and tends to appear in formal writing, but it's worth knowing. "Application" can refer to sustained, focused effort — the kind of dedicated attention you give to mastering a skill or completing a task.

  • "Her success was the result of years of application to her studies."
  • "The coach praised his players for their application during training."

Here, it means something close to "diligence" or "hard work directed at a goal." You are, in a sense, applying yourself — your energy and concentration — to something.

Every meaning of "application" involves something being directed at or put toward something else:

  • A request directed at an authority → job application
  • A substance placed onto a surface or body → application of cream
  • A theory or rule put into actual use → application of a law
  • A software tool built to perform a task → mobile application
  • Effort and focus directed at a goal → great application to one's work

This is why English uses the same word for all five things. In each case, something is being aimed, directed, or brought to bear on something else.

ContextWhat "application" means
Jobs, universities, visasA formal request
Medicine, painting, skincareThe act of putting something onto something
Science, law, skillsPractical real-world use of something
TechnologyA software program (an "app")
Work ethicFocused, sustained effort

Once you know these five meanings and the idea that ties them together — directing something at a target — you'll never be confused by this word, no matter what context you encounter it in.
924:
An appliqué is a decorative piece of material — almost always fabric — that is cut into a shape and then attached onto the surface of another, larger piece of material. The word refers both to the decorative piece itself and to the finished work that results from attaching it.

Think of it this way: imagine you have a plain blue denim jacket. Now imagine cutting a bright red rose shape out of a piece of silk, and sewing it onto the chest of that jacket. That rose is an appliqué. The decorated jacket now has an appliqué on it.

An appliqué sits on top of its background material. This means it has dimension — you can feel the layering if you run your fingers over it. It is not simply a print or a dye. It is a physical piece of material resting on another, which gives it texture and depth. This raised, layered quality is one of the defining characteristics of appliqué work.

The shapes can be anything: flowers, animals, letters, geometric forms, abstract patterns, or complex scenic scenes made up of dozens of individual fabric pieces layered together.

The appliqué piece is usually secured by stitching — either by hand or by machine — around its edges. This stitching does two things: it holds the piece firmly in place, and it often forms part of the decoration itself (a contrasting thread color, for example, can outline the shape beautifully). Sometimes an appliqué is bonded to the background using iron-on adhesive or fabric glue, though stitching is the most traditional and durable method.

The edges of the fabric shape can be handled in different ways. They might be neatly folded under and hidden before sewing (called a turned edge), left raw and intentionally frayed for a rustic effect, or completely sealed with a dense zigzag stitch called a satin stitch.

While fabric is by far the most common material, appliqués can be made from:

  • Felt — easy to work with because it doesn't fray
  • Leather or suede — gives a bold, structured look
  • Lace — for a delicate, elegant effect
  • Velvet, satin, or silk — for richness and sheen
  • Denim, wool, or cotton — for casual or rustic work

The background (the material the appliqué is placed onto) is most commonly fabric as well — a quilt, a garment, a bag, a pillow, a tablecloth, or a wall hanging.
Where You Encounter Appliqués in Real Life

Appliqués appear in an enormous variety of contexts:

In clothing and fashion: The decorative patches on children's clothing (a little elephant on a onesie, a star on a t-shirt), the embellishments on evening gowns, the brand logos sewn onto sportswear, and the decorative elements on denim jackets are all appliqués.

In quilting: Many quilts, especially traditional ones, are built almost entirely from appliqué. A quilt might feature elaborate floral appliqués, pictorial scenes, or folk-art motifs, each piece of fabric carefully cut and sewn onto the quilt top.

In home décor: Decorative pillows, tablecloths, curtains, and wall hangings often feature appliqué designs.

In accessories: Tote bags, handbags, and hats are frequently decorated with appliqués.

In flags and banners: The stars on the American flag, for instance, were historically appliquéd onto the fabric rather than printed.

In theater and costume design: Costumes often use appliqués to create the illusion of elaborate surface decoration quickly and effectively.

Over centuries of practice, several distinct approaches have developed:

Standard (or onlay) appliqué is the most common form — a piece of fabric is placed on top of the background and sewn down. This is what most people mean when they say "appliqué."

Reverse appliqué works in the opposite direction. Instead of placing fabric on top, you layer fabrics beneath the main background fabric and then carefully cut away portions of the top layer to reveal the fabric beneath. The result looks as though the design is carved into the surface. This technique is famously used by the Kuna people of Panama in their molas — brilliantly colored, layered textile panels.

Shadow appliqué places a colored fabric piece underneath a sheer or translucent top fabric. The shape becomes visible as a soft, muted silhouette showing through from below — hence "shadow."

Padded (or raised) appliqué involves adding a layer of batting, foam, or stuffing beneath the appliqué piece before sewing it down. This lifts it off the background surface and gives it a sculptural, three-dimensional quality.

Raw-edge appliqué deliberately leaves the edges of the fabric unfinished. Over time (and especially after washing), those edges fray slightly, creating a soft, textural effect that is intentional and considered part of the aesthetic.
How Appliqué Differs from Similar Things

It helps to understand appliqué by comparing it to things it resembles:

Appliqué vs. Embroidery: Embroidery decorates fabric by stitching thread directly into it — the thread is the decoration. Appliqué decorates fabric by attaching a piece of another material to it. The two techniques are often combined: an appliquéd shape might then be further embellished with embroidered details.

Appliqué vs. a Patch: A patch is often a piece of fabric sewn over a hole or worn area — its primary purpose is repair, not decoration (though it may look decorative). An appliqué's purpose is purely decorative. In everyday language, people sometimes use the words interchangeably, but technically, appliqué always refers to decorative application, not repair.

Appliqué vs. Printing: A printed design is part of the fabric itself — it has no physical depth. An appliqué is a separate object attached to the surface, always with some degree of raised texture.

An appliqué, as a noun, is a decorative piece of cut fabric (or similar material) that is attached — almost always by sewing — to the surface of a larger material to ornament it. The word can refer to the individual decorative piece, or to a finished work featuring such pieces. It is defined by its layered, surface-applied, three-dimensional nature, and it appears across clothing, quilts, home textiles, accessories, and ceremonial objects in virtually every culture in the world.
925:
Every meaning of "apply" shares one central idea — bringing something into contact with something else, with a purpose.

That "something" can be a physical substance, a rule, your effort, or even a request. But in every case, there is always a thing being directed toward a target, intentionally.

Once you hold this idea, all the meanings will feel natural.
Meaning 1: To Put Something onto a Surface

This is the most physical meaning. When you "apply" something, you deliberately place or spread it on something.

Examples:

  • Apply sunscreen to your skin before going out in the sun.
  • The nurse applied a bandage to the wound.
  • Apply a thin layer of glue to both surfaces before pressing them together.

Notice that "apply" isn't the same as simply "put." When you apply something, you usually spread it, press it, or layer it with care and intention. You apply paint with a brush. You apply pressure with your hand. The action has a deliberate, purposeful quality.
Meaning 2: To Use Something (Knowledge, a Rule, a Method) in a Situation

This is the most common meaning in academic and professional life. Here, the "thing" being applied is not physical — it's an idea, a skill, a rule, or a principle. You take it and use it in a specific situation.

Examples:

  • She applied everything she had learned in class to solve the real problem.
  • The judge applied the law fairly.
  • Apply the same logic here as you did in the previous step.
  • The company applied a 20% discount to all orders.

Think of it like this: you have a tool (knowledge, a rule, a formula), and you bring it to bear on a problem or situation. That's applying it. It's the difference between knowing something and actually using it somewhere specific.

This is why teachers say, "Don't just memorize — apply what you learn." They mean: take it out of your head and use it in real situations.
Meaning 3: To Make a Formal Request

When you "apply" for something, you formally ask an institution or organization to consider you for something — a job, a place, a visa, a loan, etc.

Examples:

  • She applied for a job at the hospital.
  • He applied to three universities and was accepted by two.
  • You need to apply for a visa before traveling to that country.
  • They applied for a loan from the bank.

Here, the "thing" being brought to a target is your request or candidacy. You take your documents, qualifications, and intentions and direct them toward an institution. The institution then decides whether to accept you.

Notice how "apply for" means you are the one seeking something, and "apply to" means you are approaching a place or organization with that request.
Meaning 4: To Be Relevant — To Concern or Relate to Something

This meaning is slightly different. Here, "apply" doesn't describe what a person does — it describes whether a rule, idea, or statement fits or is relevant to a particular person or situation.

Examples:

  • This rule applies to everyone in the building, not just new employees.
  • The discount only applies to orders above ₹500.
  • What I said earlier does not apply in your case — your situation is different.
  • These safety guidelines apply to all workers on the site.

In this sense, "apply" is almost like asking: does this thing reach this situation? Is it in effect here? Does it cover this person?

If a rule applies to you, it means it concerns you, it is relevant to you, and you must follow it. If it does not apply, it means it doesn't affect you or your situation.
Meaning 5: To Give Concentrated Effort or Attention

This meaning is about directing yourself — your focus, discipline, and energy — toward a task. You'll often see it in the phrase "apply yourself" or "apply one's mind."

Examples:

  • If you apply yourself, you can master this skill in a few months.
  • She didn't apply herself enough during the exam preparation.
  • He needs to apply his mind to this problem instead of getting distracted.
  • Apply your full attention to what the speaker is saying.

This use of "apply" is deeply purposeful. It's not about casual effort — it's about deliberately channeling your mental or physical energy into something. When someone says, "You're not applying yourself," they mean you have the ability, but you're not directing it with enough focus and seriousness.

Look at every meaning above. In every single one, there is:

  1. Something being directed — sunscreen, a rule, a request, effort, relevance.
  2. A target it is being directed toward — skin, a problem, an institution, a task, a situation.
  3. An intentional, purposeful action — not accidental, not passive.

That is the soul of the word "apply." It is always about deliberately bringing one thing to bear on another.

The word "apply" works with different prepositions, and the preposition changes the meaning slightly:

  • Apply to — to put on a surface (apply cream to skin), or to make a request to a place (apply to a university), or to be relevant to (this rule applies to you).
  • Apply for — to formally request something (apply for a job, a visa, a scholarship).
  • Apply in — to use something in a particular context (this method applies in most situations).
  • Apply oneself / apply your mind — to give focused effort (she applied herself to the work).

"Apply" suggests intentionality. You don't accidentally apply something. The word carries a sense of deliberate, directed action. This is what separates it from words like "put" or "place."

"Apply" is versatile across formality levels. It appears in everyday language (apply lotion), in professional and legal contexts (apply the law, apply for a permit), in academic settings (apply what you've learned), and in motivational speech (apply yourself). The word travels across all registers of English without sounding out of place.

"Apply" in passive form is very common:

  • "A discount was applied to your bill." (Someone applied it to your bill.)
  • "The rule is applied equally to all." (People apply the rule equally.)
  • "The pressure should be applied gently." (You should apply the pressure gently.)

In passive sentences, the action is the same — something is being brought to bear on a target — but the focus shifts to the result rather than the person doing it.

To apply means to deliberately bring something — whether a physical substance, a rule, your effort, or a formal request — into contact with or into use in relation to a specific target or situation, always with intention and purpose.
926:
To appoint someone means to officially choose them for a specific role, job, or position — and to give them that role through an act of authority.

When someone appoints another person, they are not just picking them casually. They are making a formal, deliberate decision and using their power or authority to place that person into a role.

The president appointed her as the minister of finance.

Here, the president had the authority to fill that government role, and used it to officially place her there.

The heart of the word "appoint" is authority + official designation.

Two things must be present:

  • The person doing the appointing must have the power or right to make that choice.
  • The choice must be formal and official, not just a suggestion or preference.

This is what separates appoint from simply saying "choose" or "pick." You can pick a pizza topping. You appoint a judge.
How It Is Different from Similar Words

This is where many learners get confused, so let's be very precise.

Appoint vs. Elect
When someone is elected, a group of people (voters) cast votes and the majority decides. When someone is appointed, a single authority — a boss, a president, a board, a court — makes the decision alone, without a vote.

The senator was elected by the people. (vote by many)
The senator was appointed by the governor. (decision by one authority)

Appoint vs. Hire
Hiring is a transactional process — it usually involves applications, interviews, and a mutual agreement about salary. Appointing is about the use of authority to assign a role. An appointed position often carries a sense of trust and high responsibility, and may or may not involve a formal job application process.

The company hired fifty new workers. (recruitment process)
The company's board appointed a new CEO. (a formal act of authority)

Appoint vs. Assign
Assign is more everyday and task-based — a teacher assigns homework; a manager assigns a project. Appoint is more significant and role-based — it places someone into a position, not just a task.

"Appoint" also has an older meaning: to officially fix or decide on a time or place for something. You still see this in certain fixed phrases.

At the appointed time, the ceremony began.
They met at the appointed place.

Here, "appointed" means previously decided and officially set. This use is not as common in everyday conversation, but you will encounter it in formal writing, legal contexts, and literature.

There are a few natural ways to use "appoint" in a sentence:

1. appoint someone + to + a position/role

She was appointed to the board of directors.
He was appointed to the position of chief advisor.

2. appoint someone + as + their new title

The king appointed him as the royal treasurer.
They appointed her as head of the department.

*3. appoint someone + [title directly, no "as"]

The court appointed her guardian of the child.
They appointed him chairman.

All three patterns are correct. The third pattern sounds the most formal and authoritative.

Government & Politics

The prime minister appointed a new cabinet after the election.
The president appointed three judges to the Supreme Court.

Business & Organizations

The board of directors appointed a new chief executive officer.
She was appointed head of the marketing division.

Legal

The court appointed a lawyer for the defendant who could not afford one.
A trustee was appointed to manage the estate.

Religious & Institutional

The church appointed a new bishop for the region.
The university appointed a new dean of science.
The People Involved: Key Related Words

Once you understand the verb, you should also know the words built around it:

  • Appointment (noun) — the act of appointing someone, or the position/role itself.

Her appointment as director surprised many.

  • Appointee (noun) — the person who has been appointed; the one who receives the position.

The new appointee will begin work next Monday.

  • By appointment (phrase) — arranged officially in advance; also used to indicate that a business serves clients by scheduled arrangement only.

The lawyer sees clients by appointment only.

You may come across the adjective well-appointed, especially when describing rooms, buildings, or offices. It means a space is properly and elegantly equipped or furnished — it has everything it should have, and everything is of good quality.

They stayed in a well-appointed hotel suite.
The office was modern and well-appointed.

This comes from an older use of "appoint" meaning to furnish or equip something properly. It is rarely used as a standalone verb in this sense today, but "well-appointed" as an adjective is still very much alive.

To appoint is to use your official authority to formally place a person into a specific role or position — making it clear they have been chosen, and that the choice carries weight.
927:
The word appointment is about something being formally fixed or decided — whether that's a time to meet someone, or a person being chosen for a role. Think of it as something officially locked in place.

It has three distinct meanings, and all three are commonly used in everyday English.
Meaning 1: A scheduled arrangement to meet someone at a specific time and place

This is the most common meaning in daily life.

When you and another person — often a professional — agree in advance to meet at a fixed time and place, that agreement itself is called an appointment.

"I have a doctor's appointment at 3 PM."
"She made an appointment with her lawyer for Friday."
"He missed his dentist appointment because he overslept."

A few important things to understand about this meaning:

It is always planned in advance. You don't call something an appointment if it happens spontaneously. The planning and fixing of a time is essential to the word.

It tends to be formal or semi-formal. You typically use "appointment" when meeting a doctor, dentist, lawyer, banker, counsellor, or someone in a professional setting. You would not normally say "I have an appointment with my friend to grab coffee" — for casual, informal meetings, people say plan, meetup, or simply meeting.

The appointment has a purpose. It isn't just a social visit. There is usually a clear reason for it — a check-up, a consultation, a service, etc.

Common phrases:

  • Make/book/schedule an appointment — to arrange one
  • Keep an appointment — to show up for it as planned
  • Cancel/miss an appointment — to not attend
  • By appointment only — meaning you cannot just walk in; you must schedule a time in advance
  • Appointment-only — a place or service that only sees people who have pre-arranged times
Meaning 2: The official act of choosing someone for a job, position, or role

When a person in authority officially selects or names someone for an important position, that act is called an appointment.

"The appointment of a new judge was announced yesterday."
"Her appointment as director surprised many people."
"The president's appointment of a new cabinet minister made the news."

This meaning is commonly used in professional, political, organizational, and governmental contexts.

Key things to note:

The person doing the appointing has power. A president appoints ministers. A company's board appoints a CEO. A king appoints ambassadors. The word carries a sense of authority.

It is not the same as being elected. When someone is elected, the public votes for them. When someone is appointed, a specific authority chooses them — often without a public vote.

It is formal and official. A casual choice is not an appointment. If your friend picks you to be on their quiz team, that is not an appointment. But if a university president officially names someone as dean, that is an appointment.
Meaning 3: The position or job itself that someone has been appointed to

This is closely related to Meaning 2, but here the word refers not to the act of choosing, but to the role the person now holds.

"He accepted an important government appointment."
"It was a prestigious appointment — she would be leading the entire research division."
"The appointment came with a generous salary."

In this sense, "appointment" is essentially another word for a post, position, or role — but specifically one that was given to someone by an authority, not one they applied for through a standard job process.
Meaning 4: Appointments (plural) — the furnishings and fittings of a place

This meaning is older and more formal, and you will mostly encounter it in formal writing, literature, or descriptions of grand or luxurious spaces.

When used in the plural — appointments — it can refer to the furniture, equipment, and decorative fittings that furnish a room or building.

"The hotel was known for its elegant appointments."
"The office had fine appointments — mahogany desks, leather chairs, and polished brass fixtures."

You will rarely use this meaning in everyday conversation. It appears more in formal descriptions, real estate listings for luxury properties, or literary writing. Just know it exists so you are not confused when you encounter it.

All four meanings share a common thread: something formally decided or put in place.

  • A meeting is fixed at a specific time → appointment
  • A person is officially placed in a role → appointment
  • The role they now hold → appointment
  • The fittings that are placed to furnish a space → appointments

• "I have an appointment today." (one scheduled meeting)
  • "She received a government appointment." (one official position)
  • "I have several appointments this week." (more than one scheduled meeting)
  • "The room had beautiful appointments." (furnishings — always plural in this sense)

People sometimes wonder how appointment and meeting differ.

A meeting is simply when two or more people come together to talk. It can be formal or informal, planned or spontaneous.

An appointment is always planned in advance, is almost always formal, and usually involves a professional or someone in authority. Every appointment involves a meeting of sorts — but not every meeting is an appointment.

Think of it this way: you have a meeting with a friend. You have an appointment with your doctor.
928: Apposite means perfectly suited, strikingly fitting, or precisely right for a particular situation or purpose. When something is apposite, it doesn't just connect to the topic — it matches it with a kind of sharp, elegant precision, like a key that fits a lock so perfectly that it turns without any friction at all.

This is the most important thing to understand: apposite is stronger than words like relevant, appropriate, or fitting.

Something relevant is simply connected to the subject. Something appropriate doesn't break the rules of the situation. But something apposite fits so precisely and so well that it almost feels like it was custom-made for that exact moment.

Think of it this way. Suppose you're at a friend's funeral, and someone stands up and shares a short memory about your friend that captures his entire personality in one sentence — something so spot-on that everyone in the room quietly nods and feels it. That memory, that remark, is apposite. It doesn't just fit the occasion. It hits the center of the target.
What kinds of things can be "apposite"?

This is a word almost exclusively used for things that communicate — things that express, describe, or illustrate. Think:

  • A remark or comment
  • A quotation or passage
  • An example or illustration
  • An analogy or comparison
  • An observation or response
  • A word or phrase

You wouldn't call a piece of furniture or a meal "apposite." You use it when a thought, expression, or piece of language fits a context with exceptional precision.

When apposite is connected to the thing it fits, it's followed by "to".

"She chose a quotation that was perfectly apposite to the occasion."

"His remark was apposite to everything we had been discussing."

You'll see this "apposite to..." construction frequently.
How it compares to similar words

Apt is the closest everyday equivalent. It means fitting or appropriate, and you can often swap it for apposite. But apt is more casual and more common. Apposite is more formal and implies a sharper, more impressive degree of fit. If apt means the shoe fits, apposite means the shoe fits perfectly.

Pertinent means directly relevant and to the point. It lacks the sense of elegant, precise matching that apposite carries.

Germane is very close in formality and meaning — it means directly relevant and appropriate. The difference is subtle. Germane leans toward "directly on-topic." Apposite leans toward "matched with striking precision." In practice, they can often be used interchangeably.

Fitting is more general and more casual. "A fitting tribute" just means it's appropriate. Apposite would imply something sharper and more exact.

Because they look and sound similar, learners often confuse apposite and opposite. They have absolutely nothing to do with each other in meaning.

  • Opposite means contrary, or on the other end of the spectrum. Hot is the opposite of cold.
  • Apposite means perfectly fitting and precisely suited.

These words are unrelated in meaning. The visual similarity is simply a spelling coincidence that catches many people off guard. If you can remember just one thing about this word, remember: apposite is not opposite.
Tone and register: when to use it

Apposite is a formal, somewhat literary word. You'll encounter it most often in academic writing, essays, book reviews, formal speeches, and intellectual discussion. Using it in casual conversation — "Hey, that was such an apposite thing to say!" — would feel oddly stiff and out of place. It belongs in writing and elevated speech.

"The professor's analogy was remarkably apposite — it made a difficult concept suddenly clear to everyone."

"He ended his speech with an apposite quotation from Marcus Aurelius that tied the entire argument together."

"Critics noted that the documentary's title was apposite to its central theme."

"She struggled to find an apposite word for the feeling, but nothing quite captured it."
One final image to carry with you

Imagine a sculptor carving a statue that will stand in a specific corner of a specific courtyard. A statue that is appropriate fills the space without looking wrong. But a statue that is apposite seems as though it was conceived specifically for that corner — its size, its subject, its posture, all of it speaks directly to that precise location. That feeling of "this could not be more right" is the spirit of apposite.
929:
An appraisal is a careful, considered judgment about something — its value, quality, condition, or nature. It is not a careless glance or a snap decision. It is a deliberate, thoughtful assessment formed after giving something proper attention.

Think of it this way: when you appraise something, you are essentially asking, "What is this really worth? How good is it? What is the true state of it?" — and the answer you arrive at, after thinking carefully, is the appraisal.
The Two Things the Word Can Refer To

This is important to understand because "appraisal" can mean two slightly different but related things:

1. The act (the process) of evaluating something.
For example: "The appraisal of the painting took three days."
Here, "appraisal" refers to the process — the act of examining and judging.

2. The result or conclusion of that evaluation.
For example: "The expert's appraisal was that the painting was worth $50,000."
Here, "appraisal" refers to the outcome — the actual judgment or conclusion reached.

Both meanings are correct and very common. Context will always make it clear which one is meant.
Where You'll Encounter This Word (The Main Contexts)

The word "appraisal" is used in several specific real-world situations. Here are the most important ones:

1. Financial or Property Appraisal
This is perhaps the most common use. When someone wants to know the monetary value of something — a house, a piece of art, a diamond ring, an antique, or a business — they hire a trained professional called an appraiser to examine it and determine its worth. That professional's formal valuation is called an appraisal.

Example: "Before selling their house, the family got an appraisal to find out how much it was worth on the market."

Example: "The insurance company required an appraisal of the jewellery before writing the policy."

2. Performance Appraisal
In the workplace, most organizations formally evaluate how well their employees are doing their jobs, usually once or twice a year. This structured review — where a manager assesses an employee's performance, strengths, weaknesses, and progress — is called a performance appraisal.

Example: "During her annual appraisal, her manager told her she had done outstanding work and was being considered for a promotion."

Example: "He was nervous before his appraisal because he felt he had missed some deadlines."

3. A General Assessment of a Situation, Person, or Thing
Outside of formal professional settings, "appraisal" is also used more broadly to mean any serious personal evaluation or judgment.

Example: "After a careful appraisal of the risks, she decided not to invest her savings in the startup."

Example: "His appraisal of the new employee was positive — he felt she had great potential."

Example: "The general made a quick appraisal of the situation on the battlefield."

In this sense, it simply means someone has looked at something thoughtfully and formed a well-considered opinion.

4. Critical Appraisal
You will often see the phrase "critical appraisal", especially in academic, medical, and research settings. Here, "critical" does not mean negative — it means analytical and rigorous. A critical appraisal is a systematic, careful examination of something (like a research study or an argument) to judge its quality, reliability, and value.

Example: "Medical students are trained to do a critical appraisal of research papers to determine whether the findings can be trusted."
The Key Nuance: What Separates an Appraisal from a Casual Opinion

This is crucial. Not every opinion or comment is an appraisal. An appraisal carries a sense of:

  • Care and thoroughness — it is not rushed.
  • Knowledge or expertise — it is usually made by someone who knows what they are looking at, or at least by someone who has thought about it seriously.
  • Authority or reliability — because of the above, an appraisal carries some weight and credibility.

If your friend glances at your painting and says, "Looks nice!" — that is not an appraisal. But if an experienced art dealer examines it carefully under good light, considers its style, condition, and the artist's reputation, and then tells you its market value — that is an appraisal.

The word, even when used casually, always retains this sense of genuine, considered evaluation.

Since you'll encounter these related words constantly, it helps to know them:

  • Appraise (verb) — the action. "The expert will appraise the antique tomorrow." (To appraise = to carry out an appraisal.)
  • Appraiser (noun) — the person who conducts an appraisal. "The bank sent an appraiser to inspect the property."
  • Appraisee (noun) — the person being assessed, used mainly in the context of workplace performance appraisals. "The appraisee should come prepared with examples of their achievements."
  • Appraisal (noun) — the process or result of appraising. (The word you are learning.)

• Annual appraisal — a yearly performance review at work.
  • Property appraisal — a professional valuation of real estate.
  • Independent appraisal — an assessment done by someone with no personal interest in the outcome, to ensure fairness.
  • Critical appraisal — a rigorous, analytical examination of something.
  • Appraisal of the situation — a careful reading or assessment of what is happening.
  • Self-appraisal — evaluating your own performance or qualities, often as part of a formal workplace review.

If you ever need to recall this word instantly, remember: an appraisal is a careful, expert, and considered judgment about the value or quality of something — whether that "something" is a house, an employee's work, a piece of art, or a situation unfolding in front of you.
